messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Combat Pilot
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Stop Enjoyment: give up pleasant activities, Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Daniel had spent most of his adult life in cockpits, trusting checklists, instruments, and the hard discipline of training. The accident that changed that rhythm came late in his career, during what should have been a routine flight. Something went badly wrong in the air, and in the ensuing crash he was trapped in a life-threatening situation that left him physically overwhelmed and certain, in those moments, that he might not make it out alive. In the aftermath, what stayed with him was not only the memory of the event itself but the way his body had felt during it: disoriented, lightheaded, and sick. Even now, years later, Daniel can be pulled back by the same bodily sensations. If he feels dizzy when he stands too quickly, or if he becomes physically unwell with something as ordinary as a stomach bug, he notices an immediate hardening inside himself, as if the old emergency has returned. He has also found that a sudden bang or explosion-like sound can cut through him with alarming force, making him turn sharply and scan the room before he has fully realized what he is hearing.

In the months after the accident, Daniel tried at first to keep functioning in the familiar way that had always served him. But he began quietly reshaping his life around the fear of being caught in a medical crisis again. He avoided hospitals, ambulances, and physical examinations whenever he could, insisting on postponing appointments or finding reasons not to go. Medical settings felt to him like places where danger could be confirmed rather than relieved, and he preferred to stay away from anything that made him think of tests, monitors, or being examined by strangers. His wife noticed that he would become tense simply hearing an ambulance in the distance, and he would later admit that even the thought of a hospital corridor was enough to make his stomach clench.

Daniel’s sense of himself also changed in ways he found difficult to speak about. He began describing himself as feeling “dead inside,” not in a dramatic way, but as a flat, discouraging absence of feeling that had settled over much of his life. Before the accident, he had taken pride in enjoying simple things with his wife—going out to dinner, taking drives, spending time with friends—but he gradually gave up those pleasant activities. He would say he was too tired, or that he had other things to do, though in private he admitted that he no longer trusted himself to relax. Enjoyment felt risky, almost reckless, because the world, as he had come to see it, could change in an instant. He became convinced that his old assumptions had been completely shattered. The belief that careful preparation could keep disaster at bay no longer seemed true to him, and he spoke about the world as if it had revealed itself to be fundamentally dangerous.

At home, that sense of danger showed up in the body as much as in his thoughts. Daniel described feeling constantly tense and ready to react, as if some part of him never stood down. He was increasingly hyperaware of his surroundings, watching doorways, listening for unusual sounds, and tracking movement in a way that made ordinary life feel exhausting. Unexpected movement nearby could make him flinch as if he were again in harm’s way. If his wife came up behind him without warning, or if someone moved quickly in his peripheral vision, he reacted with a startle that embarrassed him but also felt unavoidable. He understood these responses as his body staying on guard, even when his mind knew he was in his own house.

Over time, he tried to regain a sense of control in the only way that felt immediately available to him: through strict control of eating. Daniel began restricting his food carefully, measuring and limiting himself with a rigidity that his wife noticed had little to do with health and more to do with discipline. He said it helped him feel controlled when so much else did not. That same impulse also appeared in the way he organized his days. He let go of enjoyable activities one by one and narrowed his routines until life felt safer but smaller. The cost was visible in his marriage, where he became harder to reach and less likely to join in the ordinary pleasures that had once defined their shared life.

Now 56, Daniel has come for help because the strain has become impossible to ignore. His symptoms remain severe, and he is troubled by how easily a sound, a sensation of dizziness, or the sight of a medical setting can pull his attention back to danger. What brought him in was not a single crisis but the growing realization that he has been living as if the accident is still happening in some ongoing sense, with his body braced for impact and his world reduced to what can be monitored and avoided. He hopes, with some hesitation, that treatment might help him feel less trapped inside that alertness. What he fears most is that the world really has become as dangerous as it now seems to him, and that the deadened, guarded version of himself is all that is left.
